# Cakkavākajātaka (Ja 434)

**ID:** Ja 434
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Cakkavākajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Red-Ducks

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cakkavākajātaka* (Ja 434) is a canonical birth story preserved in the Jātaka collection of the Pali Canon [SuttaCentral]. Set while the Buddha was residing at Jetavana, the story was occasioned by a greedy monk (*lolabhikkhu*) who was insatiable regarding material requisites [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. In relating the past story, the narrative recounts the dialogue between a crow and a ruddy goose (*cakkavāka*, the Bodhisatta) residing with his mate in a lotus lake, contrasting the crow's scavenging diet with the virtuous restraint and mutual devotion of the geese [Fausböll 1883]. At the conclusion of the sermon, after the declaration of the Four Noble Truths, the greedy monk attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), and the characters of the past are identified: the crow was the greedy monk, the female goose was Rāhulamātā, and the male goose was the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1883]. In secondary scholarship on the Buddha legend, the text is cited for the Buddha instructing his disciples on the four foundations of mindfulness, the Noble Eightfold Path, and nine transcendent conditions that overcome Māra [Khosla 1989].

Care must be taken to distinguish Ja 434 from another homonymous story, Ja 451 (also titled *Cakkavākajātaka*), which shares a similar motif of a crow questioning a ruddy goose but contains different verses. Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus identifies substantial internal overlap between Ja 434 and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (10 matching segments, up to 95% similarity) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also records weak cross-language alignments with the Sanskrit *Kāraṇḍavyūhasūtra* and a Tibetan canonical text, though SuttaCentral lists no direct external parallels [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
